# What a sugar tax on soft drinks changes

*Test fixture written for this repo. The numbers are illustrative.*

Several countries tax sugary soft drinks to cut how much sugar people drink. A typical design adds 20% to the shelf price of drinks with a lot of added sugar.

Shops pass most of the tax on to customers: studies find prices rise by about 80% of the tax. Buyers respond. For every 10% rise in price, people buy about 12% less of the taxed drinks, according to a large review of studies.

Makers respond too. Faced with the tax, many reformulate their drinks to fall below the sugar threshold. In one country, the sugar in soft drinks sold fell by about 30% within three years, mostly because recipes changed, not because people bought fewer drinks.

The money raised goes to the government. In some places it funds school sport or healthy meals.

A common belief is that the tax works mainly by making people buy less. In practice, the biggest effect often comes from companies changing recipes before the tax even starts.

The tax has costs. It takes a larger share of income from poorer households, who drink more soft drinks. People can switch to untaxed sugary foods. And drinks just under the threshold still contain sugar.
